# Data sources {#data-sources .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Section 1
:::

::: notes
Section one. Data reach a researcher by one of three routes, and the vocabulary of the archives follows those routes. We take the routes first, then the places that hold most of the quantitative data of sociology, political science and demography, with the access rule of each. Then the four cases of the course, which between them use two of the three routes, and the terms of the archive whose rules shape one of the cases more than any other.
:::

## Three routes to data {#three-routes-to-data .smaller}

::: {.fs-75}
| Route | What it asks of you | Typical sources |
|:-----|:-----------|:-----------|
| **Open download** | the citation, under a licence that permits reuse: CC BY, CC0 or an open government licence | World Bank indicators, the aggregate tables of Eurostat, the public-use files of the US statistical agencies, most replication packages |
| **Registration and licence** | an account in your own name, and conditions such as no redistribution and no attempt to identify anyone | survey microdata: the European Social Survey, the Eurobarometer at GESIS, the safeguarded collection of the UK Data Service |
| **Application and secure access** | a project description, often accreditation, then a file sent under contract or work in a secure environment | the microdata of Eurostat, the UK Data Service through SecureLab, the Secure Research Service of the ONS |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
A file with one row per respondent needs the second or third route, while the country-year tables computed from it are usually open.
:::

::: {.src}
The modules Social science data sources of the case sites, section 1, from the access pages of the archives.
:::

::: notes
Almost every dataset that you will use comes by one of three routes. The first is open download: a public page or an interface for programs, a licence that permits reuse, and nothing asked of you except the citation. The second asks for an account in your own name and your agreement to conditions, typically no passing the files on and no attempt to identify anyone. That is the standard route for survey microdata. The third is for data too detailed to leave the archive: you apply with a project, may have to become an accredited researcher, and work in a secure setting, and access can take weeks or months. [advance] The line between microdata and aggregates runs across all three routes, and it decides what a reanalysis may share.
:::

## Where the data are held {#where-the-data-are-held .smaller}

::: {.fs-75}
| Source | What it holds | Access |
|:-----|:-----------|:-------|
| **European Social Survey** | attitudes, values and behaviour across Europe, every two years since 2002 | registration, free |
| **Eurobarometer**, at GESIS | surveys run twice a year for the European Commission since 1974 | registration with GESIS, free for academic use |
| **ISSP**, **EVS** and **WVS** | themed modules and values surveys in many countries | registration, free |
| **UK Data Service** | the large UK government surveys, the household panels and the cohorts | three tiers: open, safeguarded, controlled |
| **NCHS** | the national health surveys of the United States, the National Survey of Family Growth among them | open, without registration, under its data use restrictions |
| **Eurostat** | the aggregate statistics of the EU by country, region and year, and fourteen collections of microdata | aggregates open, microdata by application |
| **World Bank**, **OECD**, **ILOSTAT** | indicators by country and year | open |
| **CESSDA**, **re3data** | catalogues that say where a dataset is held | open |
:::

::: {.src}
The modules Social science data sources of the case sites, section 2, which give the addresses.
:::

::: notes
This is a map rather than a census, drawn from the module that is the reading of this session, which has the full tables with their addresses. Four kinds of source matter most for us. The cross-national survey programmes, the European Social Survey, the Eurobarometer, the ISSP and the values surveys, all ask for a free registration. The national archives, such as the UK Data Service, sort their holdings into tiers, from open download to a secure lab. The official statistical offices publish their aggregates openly and keep the microdata behind applications. And the international organisations publish indicators by country and year that anyone can download. A catalogue such as CESSDA tells you that a dataset exists and where it is held, and you then register with the archive that holds it.
:::

## The data of the four cases {#the-data-of-the-four-cases .smaller}

::: {.fs-75}
| Case | The data, and where they are held | Route and terms | What a reanalysis may share |
|:----|:-----------|:-----------|:---------|
| Housing audit | the 1,014 emails of the field experiment, deposited on the Harvard Dataverse by the original authors (OAs) | open download; CC0, a dedication to the public domain | the file itself |
| Immigration and trust | rounds 1 to 4 of the European Social Survey, from the ESS Data Portal | registration, free; CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | a derived extract under the same licence, cited as "Adapted from ESS" |
| Cohabitation | the public-use files of the National Survey of Family Growth, from the National Center for Health Statistics | open download, without registration; public domain, under the NCHS data use restrictions | derived files |
| EU frames | sixteen Eurobarometer waves held by GESIS; unemployment and growth from the World Bank and Eurostat | registration and a licence for the waves; open, with attribution, for the series | country-year aggregates only, under CC BY 4.0 |
:::

::: {.src}
The facts file of each case; the modules Social science data sources of the housing and EU sites.
:::

::: notes
The four cases of the course use two of the three routes, and together the cases make a good tour of the terms. The housing-audit file is the easy one: the original authors, the OAs, deposited it on the Harvard Dataverse under CC0, so anyone may copy and redistribute it, and the course ships it as it is. The European Social Survey asks for a free registration, and its data are licensed for non-commercial use with attribution and share-alike, so a derived extract can travel under the same licence, marked as adapted. The National Survey of Family Growth is in the public domain and needs no registration at all, under a short list of rules that protect the respondents. And the EU-frames case rests on the most restrictive terms of the four, which are on the next slide.
:::

## The terms of a licensed archive {#the-terms-of-a-licensed-archive .smaller}

::: {.claimcard .fs-80}
"The provision of the database to third parties is not permitted"
:::

::: {.claimcard .fs-80}
"The presentation or publication of individual cases, even if there is no direct reference to individuals, is not permitted", while "summary presentations of data, as is customary in scientific papers and lectures, are permitted"
:::

::: {.claimcard .fs-80}
"The use of AI systems for processing the database provided to the user by GESIS is prohibited"
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
So the EU-frames case shares country-year aggregates only, and the respondent files stay on the machine of each person who downloads them.
:::

::: {.src}
The terms of use of GESIS, valid since 4 February 2026, as quoted in the module Social science data sources of the EU-frames site, section 3.1.
:::

::: notes
These are three clauses from the terms of use to which every GESIS download dialog links, in the version valid since February 2026. The first forbids passing the files on to anyone, and the terms name repositories and archives among the third parties. The second draws the line along which the EU-frames case is built: no individual cases, while summary presentations of the kind found in papers and lectures are allowed, which is why the course can publish its panel of country-years. The third bears on how you work: the respondent files may not be processed with an AI system. The module on AI assistants on this site sets out what that means in practice, and the EU-frames workspace switches the AI features of Positron and VS Code off for its whole folder.
:::

## Fetching data from code {#fetching-data-from-code .deepdive run="fetch"}

::: {.fs-90}
``` r
deposit <- dataverse::get_dataframe_by_name(
  "HousingAuditAJPSFinalPublic_Unidentified.tab",
  dataset  = "doi:10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU",
  server   = "dataverse.harvard.edu",
  original = TRUE,             # the Stata file as deposited, not the tab-separated copy
  .f       = haven::read_dta   # the function that reads it
)

macro <- WDI::WDI(country = c("DE", "FR", "GB"),
                  indicator = c(unemp = "SL.UEM.TOTL.NE.ZS", growth = "NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG"),
                  start = 2004, end = 2013)
```
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
No call of this kind reaches the Eurobarometer: GESIS registers each user through a web form with a captcha, and asks for a purpose of use at every download.
:::

::: {.src}
The second page of the module Getting started with R on this site.
:::

::: notes
When the route is open, the download can be written down in your script instead of clicked through on a website, and that is what makes it repeatable. The first call reads the data file of the housing-audit case straight from its record on the Harvard Dataverse, in the Stata format in which the OAs deposited it. The second asks the World Bank for the unemployment rate and the growth of the economy in three countries, from 2004 to 2013. Both calls appear, shown but not run, in the second part of the module on R on this site. [advance] The Eurobarometer offers no such interface. Registration is a web form with a captcha, and every download asks for a purpose of use in your own name, so those files are clicked, not scripted.
:::

# Repositories {#repositories .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Section 2
:::

::: notes
Section two turns to the other side of the exchange: where a finished piece of work is deposited, so that another person can find it, cite it and run it again. We start with what a repository has to do, which gives a checklist for choosing one, then the repositories that researchers actually use, and the difference between a code forge such as GitHub and an archive. We end on a change that touches every record of this course, since the Open Science Framework is closing its projects to new work.
:::

## What a repository has to do {#what-a-repository-has-to-do .smaller}

::: {.fs-80}
| Property | What it means |
|:-------|:---------------|
| **A persistent identifier** | a DOI that resolves to the deposit for as long as the repository exists, and that a paper can cite |
| **Versions** | a new version gets a new identifier or number, while the old one still resolves |
| **A licence** | a statement of what others may do with the deposit |
| **Metadata** | a title, creators, a description and dates, in a form that catalogues can read |
| **Preservation** | a commitment, usually institutional, to keep the files readable over decades |
| **Access control** | public by default, with embargoes, restricted files or private links for reviewers |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
A folder on a laptop, a departmental server and a link in the appendix of a paper do none of these six things.
:::

::: {.src}
The modules Reproducibility repositories of the case sites, section 1.
:::

::: notes
Here is the checklist, six things that a repository does and a folder on your laptop does not. A persistent identifier, usually a DOI, which a paper can cite and which keeps resolving. Versions, so that the reader who follows the citation gets the version that the paper used. A licence, which tells others what they may do, and which the licence of the data underneath can limit. Metadata, which decides whether anyone who was not sent the link will ever find the deposit. Preservation, a commitment to keep the files readable for decades, which most archives of the social sciences have had certified. And access control, from fully public to an embargo or a private link for a reviewer.
:::

## The repositories that researchers use {#the-repositories-that-researchers-use .smaller}

::: {.fs-75}
| Repository | What it takes | Identifier and versions | Cost |
|:-------|:-----------|:-----------|:--------|
| **Zenodo** | any research output: data, code, slides, reports | a DOI for each version, and a concept DOI for all versions | free, hosted by CERN |
| **Harvard Dataverse** | datasets with their documentation, in collections for journals and projects | a DOI for each dataset and each file, with numbered versions | free at Harvard |
| **Figshare** | datasets, code, figures, presentations | a DOI for each item and version | free for individuals |
| **Dryad** | curated data that accompany a journal article | a DOI | a charge, often paid by the journal or the institution |
| **UK Data Service ReShare** | data from UK projects, those funded by the ESRC above all | a persistent identifier | free |
| **OSF** | registrations and preprints; projects until February 2027 | a DOI for public registrations | free |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Beside these repositories sit the archives of the disciplines, such as the UK Data Service, GESIS, ICPSR and the Qualitative Data Repository, and the repositories that universities run for their own staff.
:::

::: {.src}
The modules Reproducibility repositories of the case sites, section 2, from the guide of the Center for Open Science on choosing a repository.
:::

::: notes
These are the generalist repositories that most social scientists meet. Zenodo takes anything and gives every version its own DOI, and it can archive each release of a GitHub repository automatically. The Harvard Dataverse is built for datasets and lets a journal keep a collection of its own, which is how the American Journal of Political Science keeps its replication packages, the housing-audit package among them. Figshare is quick to use, Dryad charges for curation, and ReShare is the route that satisfies the data policy of the ESRC. Which one to use depends on what you deposit: a dataset goes to the archive of its discipline if there is one, and to Dataverse or Zenodo otherwise, while code goes to a forge, which is the next slide.
:::

## Code forges and archives {#code-forges-and-archives .smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**A forge** such as GitHub, GitLab or Codeberg hosts a git repository, in which code is written, reviewed and shared.

It has no DOI, it can be renamed or deleted by its owner in a minute, and it carries no commitment to preservation.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**An archive** such as Zenodo takes a tagged release of that repository and gives it a DOI, a fixed version and a commitment to keep serving it.

A paper cites the archived release, and the forge keeps the working copy.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.src}
The modules Reproducibility repositories of the case sites, section 3.
:::

::: notes
GitHub and its relatives are where most research code is found, which makes them look like repositories in the sense of the checklist, but they lack most of its properties. A GitHub repository has no DOI, it can be renamed, transferred or deleted by its owner in a minute, and nobody has promised to keep it. The remedy is cheap and standard: tag a release on the forge and let Zenodo archive it, which gives that release a DOI that a paper can cite, while the forge keeps the working copy that goes on changing. The module on Git and GitHub on this site takes you from nothing to a repository of your own, and the third day of the Extended course puts your own report under Git.
:::

## Versions of a record {#versions-of-a-record .deepdive run="versions"}

::: {.small}
- **Dataverse** numbers its versions. The package of the housing-audit OAs went up as version 1.0 on 17 February 2016, while the article was forthcoming, and version 1.1 of 23 April 2017 completed the citation, with every file unchanged
- **The OSF** keeps every revision of a file, and nothing in a registration can change once it is submitted
- **Zenodo** gives each version a DOI of its own, and a concept DOI that always points at the latest
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
A citation names the version that it used, so that its reader gets what the paper used.
:::

::: {.src}
The modules Reproducibility repositories of the housing and EU sites, section on versions.
:::

::: notes
A deposit changes after it is made, and a good repository keeps every state of it. The housing-audit package shows the pattern on Dataverse: version one point zero went up in February 2016, before the article appeared in print, and version one point one followed in April 2017, only to complete the citation, with every file the same to the byte. The OSF keeps the revisions of each file, which is why the SCORE replication of the EU-frames claim, whose report was revised in October 2026, still shows both of its reports. Zenodo gives every version a DOI of its own. Whichever repository you use, cite the version, because the reader who follows your citation should get what you used.
:::

## The OSF after 2026 {#the-osf-after-2026}

::: {.small}
- **27 August 2026.** The Center for Open Science announced that OSF Projects are being phased out, since keeping them running would require raising about four to five million dollars a year
- **From 16 November 2026.** No new projects, and no new components of existing projects
- **From 19 February 2027.** Every project is read-only, at the same addresses and DOIs
- **Unaffected.** "Registrations & Preregistrations and Preprints are unaffected by this change"
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
For new work, the OSF holds the plan and the links, and the data and the code go to a repository of the kinds on the previous slides.
:::

::: {.src}
The help pages of the OSF on the transition, as quoted in the modules Reproducibility repositories of the case sites, section on the OSF after 2026.
:::

::: notes
This change touches every record of this course. On the twenty-seventh of August 2026 the Center for Open Science announced that it is phasing out OSF Projects, the workspaces in which SCORE and Multi100 kept their records, because it cannot sustain what the projects cost to run. From the sixteenth of November 2026 nobody can create a new project, and from the nineteenth of February 2027 every project is read-only. Nothing in the records of this course is lost, because the SCORE projects of the four cases are public and stay readable at the same addresses. Registrations and preprints carry on as before. For new work the arrangement changes: the plan is registered on the OSF, and the data and code go to a repository such as Zenodo or Dataverse, linked from the registration.
:::

# Registrations {#registrations .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Section 3
:::

::: notes
Section three is about the other thing that the OSF keeps: registrations, which freeze a plan with a date on it before the result is known. An archive freezes materials and a registration freezes a plan, and the two dates, of the plan and of the result, are what let a reader tell an analysis planned in advance from one chosen after the fact. We look at what a registration is and at one that did its job in a case of the course, then at the preregistration of Multi100 itself, and last at the two templates that a reanalysis can use.
:::

## Registrations {#every-reanalysis-leaves-a-public-trail}

::: {.small}
- A registration is "a frozen version of your project that can never be edited or deleted, but you can issue a withdrawal of it later"
- It is time-stamped, with an identifier of its own, a DOI once public, and an embargo of up to four years if needed
- For new data, it fixes the plan before the data are collected; for a reanalysis, before the analytical choices are made
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The replication of the housing-audit claim uploaded its preregistration on 5 May 2020, registered it on 14 May 2020 under an embargo until 13 May 2024 (osf.io/v6wd8), and uploaded its final report on 7 October 2020, so the plan came first.
:::

::: {.src}
The help pages of the OSF on registrations; the SCORE project of the housing-audit paper, osf.io/3a8bg.
:::

::: notes
A registration is what the OSF calls a frozen document. In the words of its help pages, it is a frozen version of your project that can never be edited or deleted, though you can withdraw it later. It carries a timestamp and an identifier, gets a DOI once it is public, and can stay private under an embargo of up to four years. That is the mechanism behind preregistration. For new data it records the plan before the data are collected, and for a reanalysis, before the specific choices are made. [advance] Here is one that did its job, in the housing-audit case: the replication registered its plan in May 2020, kept it under embargo while the work ran, and reported in October. Because the plan is dated before the report, nobody can say that the analysis was chosen to fit the result.
:::

## The Multi100 preregistration {#the-study-you-are-inside-was-preregistered}

::: {.small}
- Multi100 was preregistered on the OSF after its analysts had been recruited and before any analysis began
- The registration fixed the aim, the two questions and the rule for comparing effect sizes: a new result counts as different when it lies beyond ±0.05 Cohen's *d* of the original
- A second preregistration covered the peer evaluation of the reanalyses
- The outcome: 74% of the reanalyses reached the same conclusion, and 34% came within ±0.05 *d*
:::

::: {.src}
Preregistrations osf.io/4ev9t (pp. 2 and 9) and osf.io/y4evp; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness [p. 136].
:::

::: notes
Multi100 practised what it measured. Its first preregistration was filed after the analysts had been recruited and before any of them had started, and it fixed the questions and, above all, the judging: two results count as the same when their effect sizes lie within five hundredths of a Cohen's d. It even explains why it sets confidence intervals aside, since a less precise estimate would look more robust. A second registration covered the peer evaluation. That is why the seventy-four per cent and the thirty-four per cent of the last session mean something, because nobody could move the goalposts once the results were in. The course repeats this design on the second day, with you as a sixth analyst who declares an analysis before running it.
:::

## Preregistration templates {#two-templates-one-choice}

::: {.small}
- **The AsPredicted form**, on the OSF as the "Preregistration Template from AsPredicted.org": eight short questions, from whether any data have been collected to the sample size. The preregistration block of the course follows it, adapted for data already in hand
- **The template for secondary data**: 25 questions, written for the analysis of existing data, among them questions on what you already know about the data and their results [@VandenAkkerEtAl2021PreregistrationSecondaryData, p. 3]
- Both are set out in the reading of this session
:::

::: notes
Two templates matter for a reanalysis. The AsPredicted form asks eight questions in plain language, and the preregistration block of the course follows it. But it was written for people who have not collected their data yet, and its first question, whether any data have been collected, has for us the awkward answer that we already hold everything. The template that van den Akker and colleagues wrote for secondary data is built for exactly that situation: twenty-five questions, among them a set on what you already know about the data and how you came to know it. A preregistration of a reanalysis cannot promise that you approached the data blind, only that your choices were fixed and dated before you ran them, and the block of the course borrows that part as its data-in-hand statement.
:::

# The public record {#the-public-record .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Section 4
:::

::: notes
Section four puts the morning together. SCORE kept everything that it did with each paper in one public tree of projects on the OSF, and Multi100 left its records in the same trees and in a public dataset of its own. Reading such a record is a skill in itself, and you practise it on the record of the case of your course. We end on the route by which you would deposit a reanalysis of your own, so that it leaves a record of the same kind.
:::

::: {.src}
The facts file of each case; the modules Reproducibility repositories of the housing and EU sites.

## Reading a dossier {#reading-a-dossier .questionslide}

::: {.none .nonincremental}
Open the SCORE project of the case of your course. No account is needed.

- Which components does it hold, and which of the three Rs does each one test?
- Open the Multi100 component and one analyst inside it: what did the analyst leave behind?
- Find the replication: does it have a preregistration, and is the plan dated before the report?
:::

::: notes
Now you read a record yourselves. Open the SCORE project of the case of your course, from the addresses on the last slide; everything there is public, and you need no account. Work through the three questions in order. First the map: which components are there, and which of the three Rs each one tests. Then one analyst of Multi100: did the analyst leave code, data, a report, or all three? Then the replication: look for its preregistration and its report, and compare their dates. Take the time you need. When we compare what you found, notice how the records differ, because the differences tell you how far each kind of check could go in your case. [wait]
:::

## Depositing a reanalysis of your own {#depositing-a-reanalysis}

::: {.small .fs-85}
1. **The code goes on a forge**, with a licence file and a README that says what the repository is
2. **Each version that you cite is archived** by a release on Zenodo, which gives it a DOI
3. **The data go where their licence allows.** Public-domain data travel with the code, and data that may not be passed on stay on your machine, with a README that says how to obtain them
4. **The plan goes on OSF Registries** before the analysis runs, with the DOIs of the code and data in its Resources fields
5. **The rendered report is part of the release**, so that the numbers shown are those that the code produced
6. **The data are cited** with their version and the date of download
:::

::: {.src}
The modules Reproducibility repositories of the case sites, last section.
:::

::: notes
Put together, the session gives a route for depositing a reanalysis like the one that you build in this course, and it works after the change at the OSF as well as before it. The code goes on a forge, with a licence and a README. Each version that you want to cite is archived on Zenodo, which gives it a DOI. The data go where their licence allows: the housing-audit file can travel with the code, while the Eurobarometer files never leave your machine. The plan is registered before the analysis runs, with links to the archived code and data. The rendered report goes into the release, and the data are cited with their versions. <script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
